figures.caption: Figure 4: Confusion matrices for the 4 main conditions. The Direct condition shows systematic off-diagonal mass in the ANSWER row (overcommitment). The Confidence-Only condition shows mass in the ABSTAIN column (deferral collapse). Action-Only and PSC are nearly diagonal.
Figure 3: Action accuracy (solid) vs. content adequacy (transparent) by condition. Content adequacy is strictly ≤ accuracy, validating the metric’s strictness.

Table 4: Ablation results. Removing either PSC dimension causes targeted degradation: PSC−Support loses REQUEST SUPPORT accuracy; PSC−Evidence triggers large-scale overcommitment on unsupported items.

Figure 6: Ablation comparison across three metrics. Removing support-sufficiency degrades typed deferral without increasing overcommitment. Removing evidence-sufficiency causes a 4.5× surge in overcommitment.
Figure 7: Ablation confusion matrices. PSC−Support shows all support-blocked items falling to ABSTAIN. PSC−Evidence shows all unsupported items falling to ANSWER.

Table 1: The 8 task families in SSTA-32. Each family generates 4 counterfactual variants (Complete, Clarifiable, Support-Blocked, Unsupported-Now), yielding 32 evaluation items. The dataset is perfectly balanced: 8 items per support state.

Figure 5: Per-family accuracy across the four conditions. The Direct condition shows consistent degradation across families, while structured conditions achieve near-perfect family-level scores. The Code family shows a characteristic boundary case even under structured prompting.

Figure 1: Overcommitment and typed deferral accuracy across the four main conditions. Direct execution overcommits on 41.7% of non-complete items. Structured prompting (Action-Only, PSC) reduces this to 8.3% while achieving 91.7% typed deferral.
Figure 2: Per-state action accuracy heat map. Complete items are handled well across conditions. The key differentiator is the model’s ability to distinguish between the three non-complete states.
